summaryEn: The world's largest maker of replacement headlamps — the part every collision repair needs and no carmaker wants sold by anyone else. Mercedes-Benz sued it over design rights and won at second instance; the Supreme Court has since sent the case back for retrial.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; aftermarket-lamp framing — the global position, 33.5% gross margin and strong cash generation credited, with the Mercedes design-right litigation reported accurately including the ~NT$18.12m second-instance award and the Supreme Court remand, but FY2025's 26.4% EPS decline stated with its attributed causes, and 2025Q2's 1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin flagged as a large non-operating charge whose composition was NOT verified and is NOT asserted; sector 汽車工業 → Automotive Lighting (Aftermarket))

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Depo Auto Parts (帝寶工業, TWSE: 6605) makes **replacement automotive lamps** — the headlamps and tail lamps fitted when a damaged car is repaired. Founded in **1980** in Tainan and **listed in March 2004**, it is the world's largest producer in the **automotive aftermarket** for lighting, supplying repair shops and parts distributors across Europe, North America and Asia under the **DEPO** brand.

The business exists because of a structural feature of car ownership: **lamps are among the first things damaged in a collision**, they are expensive when bought from the vehicle manufacturer, and an independent alternative saves the owner — or the insurer — a great deal of money. Depo's product is functionally equivalent and considerably cheaper. This makes it valuable to consumers and insurers, and unwelcome to carmakers, who earn high margins on original replacement parts.

That tension has produced the litigation the company is best known for. **Mercedes-Benz sued Depo over design rights** covering headlamp shapes. At **second instance the court found infringement and awarded compensation of about NT$18.12m**; Depo appealed, arguing among other things for a statutory **"repair clause" exemption** of the kind that exists in several jurisdictions to permit independent production of replacement parts. **The Supreme Court has since remanded the case for retrial**, and the dispute has broadened from straightforward infringement toward questions of **whether the carmaker's conduct is anti-competitive and what rights consumers have to repair their own vehicles**. The worst outcome originally feared — a production ban and very large damages — is generally seen as having passed, though the matter is not concluded.

Financially the company is solid and currently in a soft patch. Annual EPS ran **NT$10.86 (FY2022) → 14.29 → 18.97 (FY2024) → NT$13.97 (FY2025)** — a **26.4% decline** in FY2025 that the company's coverage attributes to **tariffs, New Taiwan dollar appreciation and non-operating losses**. **2026Q1 EPS was NT$4.41**, down from NT$5.04. Gross margin remains strong at **33.5%** and operating margin at **18.3%**, and **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$1.32bn comfortably exceeded NT$734m of net profit**. The balance sheet is conservative — **NT$33.5bn of assets on NT$21.1bn of equity, a 36.9% debt ratio and NT$3.98bn of cash** — with **trailing return on equity of 10.50%**.

**One quarter needs flagging.** In **2025Q2 the net margin was 1.5% against an operating margin of 18.0%** — implying a very large non-operating charge, since EPS collapsed to **NT$0.44** while operations remained profitable. **The composition of that charge could not be independently verified and is not asserted here.**

At **NT$130.00 the shares trade at 9.75× earnings and 1.05× book with a 5.00% yield** — essentially at book value. The honest read: **a globally dominant supplier of a genuinely useful product, structurally opposed by its own end market's manufacturers, currently earning less than it did in 2024 and priced as though the litigation risk has not gone away.**

Depo was founded in **1980** in Tainan, in the cluster of southern Taiwanese firms that supply automotive replacement parts. The **automotive aftermarket** — parts sold for repair rather than for new vehicle assembly — was then, and remains, a very large and unglamorous industry. When a car is damaged, someone must supply a replacement bumper, fender, mirror or lamp, and the vehicle manufacturer's own part is typically the most expensive option available.

Taiwan became unusually good at this. Companies like Depo and **Tong Yang (1319)**, also in this collection, built global positions by producing parts that fit and function like the original at a fraction of the price — supplying repair shops, distributors and insurers across Europe and North America. Insurers in particular became important allies: an insurer paying for a repair has a direct financial interest in a cheaper part that performs the same job.

Depo specialised in **lighting** — headlamps and tail lamps — which is a demanding product. A headlamp must meet **regulatory standards for beam pattern and intensity**, survive weather and vibration for years, and **fit the vehicle's bodywork exactly**. Getting all three right for hundreds of vehicle models requires substantial tooling, optical engineering and testing. Depo did, and became the **world's largest aftermarket automotive lamp maker**. It **listed in 2004**.

The success created the conflict. **Vehicle manufacturers earn high margins on original replacement parts**, and lamps are among the most valuable. Their defence has been **design rights** — arguing that a replacement lamp shaped to fit their car copies their protected design. **Mercedes-Benz brought exactly that case against Depo**, and at **second instance won a finding of infringement with compensation of about NT$18.12m**.

Depo's counter-argument is the one used across the industry: a replacement part must copy the original's shape **because it has to fit** — and many jurisdictions therefore have a **"repair clause"** permitting it. Depo appealed, campaigned publicly for such legislation in Taiwan, and **the Supreme Court remanded the case for retrial**. The question has since widened into whether restricting independent replacement parts is itself anti-competitive.

- **1980 (25 April)** — Depo Auto Parts founded in Tainan, making automotive lamps for the replacement market.
- **1980s–2000s** — Builds a global aftermarket lighting position, supplying repair shops, distributors and insurers in Europe, North America and Asia under the **DEPO** brand.
- **2004 (17 March)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (6605)**.
- **2010s–2020s** — **Mercedes-Benz brings design-right litigation** against Depo over headlamp designs, a case widely viewed in Taiwan as a test of the entire aftermarket parts industry.
- **2022 (July)** — **Second-instance ruling: infringement found, compensation of about NT$18.12m.** Depo announces it will appeal and calls publicly for legislation creating a **repair-clause exemption**.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$10.86**; dividend **NT$5.0**.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$14.29**; dividend **NT$6.5**.
- **2024** — Best recent year: **FY2024 EPS NT$18.97**; dividend raised to **NT$9.0**.
- **2025Q2** — **EPS collapses to NT$0.44** on a **1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin** — a large non-operating charge, composition not independently verified.
- **2025** — **FY2025 EPS NT$13.97**, down **26.4%**, attributed to tariffs, New Taiwan dollar appreciation and non-operating losses; dividend cut to **NT$6.5**.
- **Litigation status** — **The Supreme Court remands the case for retrial**; the worst-feared outcome of a production ban and very large damages is generally viewed as having passed, with the dispute broadening to competition and consumer repair-rights questions.
- **2026Q1** — **EPS NT$4.41** (from NT$5.04); gross margin **33.5%**, operating margin **18.3%**; operating cash flow **NT$1.32bn** against **NT$734m** of net profit.

Depo's accounts show **a strongly profitable niche manufacturer having a difficult year, with one quarter that needs explaining**.

- **Earnings peaked in FY2024 and fell in FY2025.** Annual EPS: **NT$10.86 (FY2022) → 14.29 (FY2023) → 18.97 (FY2024) → NT$13.97 (FY2025)** — a **26.4% decline**, attributed in coverage of the company to **tariffs, New Taiwan dollar appreciation and non-operating losses**. **2026Q1 EPS of NT$4.41** was below the prior year's **NT$5.04**.
- **The quarter that distorts the year.** **2025Q2 produced EPS of just NT$0.44 on a 1.5% net margin — against an operating margin of 18.0%.** Operations were normally profitable; something below the operating line removed almost all of it. A charge of that size is consistent with a large foreign-exchange loss during a period of New Taiwan dollar appreciation, but **the composition was not independently verified and is not asserted here**. Excluding that quarter, FY2025 would have looked substantially better.
- **The underlying operating margins are strong and stable.** Gross margin: **33.5% (2024Q4) → 34.9% → 32.7% → 25.8% → 32.1% → 33.5% (2026Q1)**. Operating margin: **18.6% → 18.3%**, with a single dip to 11.7%. For a replacement-parts manufacturer these are excellent, and they indicate genuine pricing power rather than commodity supply.
- **Cash generation is strong.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$1.32bn** against **NT$734m of net income** — a ratio near 1.8×, which is what a well-run manufacturer with substantial depreciation should produce.
- **A conservative balance sheet.** **NT$33.5bn of assets** on **NT$21.1bn of equity** — a **36.9% debt ratio** — with **NT$3.98bn of cash**. **Trailing return on equity is 10.50%.**
- **A dividend that follows earnings.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$1.4 (2020) → 3.0 → 5.0 (2022) → 6.5 (2023) → NT$9.0 (2024) → NT$6.5 (2025)**. The **5.00% yield** at NT$130.00 sits on a payout of roughly **47%** of FY2025 earnings — comfortable.
- **Priced at book.** **9.75× earnings and 1.05× book.** For a company with 33% gross margins and 10.5% ROE, trading at book value reflects the market's discount for **litigation and trade-policy uncertainty**.

The financing reality: **a high-margin niche leader with strong cash flow and a conservative balance sheet, valued at book because of risks that sit outside its operations.**

**Stance: the world's largest aftermarket automotive lamp maker, earning 33% gross margins with strong cash flow, at 9.75x earnings and book value — discounted for litigation and trade risk rather than for how the business performs.**

The bull case:

1. **A genuinely dominant global position in a hard product.** Headlamps must meet **regulatory beam standards, survive years of weather and vibration, and fit exactly** — across hundreds of vehicle models. Depo has the tooling, optics and testing to do it at scale, which is why it leads the aftermarket worldwide.
2. **Structural demand.** Cars are damaged and repaired continuously, and lamps are among the most commonly replaced parts. **Insurers and consumers have a direct financial interest** in a cheaper alternative to the manufacturer's own part.
3. **Strong economics.** **Gross margin 33.5%, operating margin 18.3%**, **operating cash flow 1.8× net income**, a **36.9% debt ratio**, **NT$3.98bn of cash** and a **5.00% yield** at roughly a 47% payout.
4. **The worst litigation outcome appears to have passed.** The **Supreme Court remanded the Mercedes case for retrial**, and the argument has broadened toward **competition policy and consumer repair rights** — terrain considerably more favourable to Depo than pure design-right infringement.

The counter-arguments:

- **Litigation is unresolved.** The second-instance court **found infringement**, with compensation of about **NT$18.12m** — small in itself, but the precedent matters far more than the sum. An adverse final outcome would affect the entire Taiwanese aftermarket parts industry.
- **FY2025 earnings fell 26.4%**, attributed to **tariffs, currency appreciation and non-operating losses**, and 2026Q1 was below the prior year.
- **One quarter's non-operating charge is unexplained.** **2025Q2's 1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin** — the composition was not verifiable from public sources.
- **Trade policy exposure.** Depo exports globally; tariffs and currency movements hit reported results directly, as FY2025 demonstrated.
- **Revenue is flat to negative** — monthly revenue has run **−14% to +8%**.

A **discounted-quality** thesis: an excellent business at book value, where the discount is for legal and policy risk rather than operational weakness — and where that risk is real but appears to be narrowing.

Depo makes and sells **replacement automotive lamps**, and its economics turn on a specific structural conflict:

- **The product.** Headlamps and tail lamps for **collision repair** — sold to repair shops, parts distributors and, indirectly, insurers, rather than to vehicle manufacturers for new car assembly. When a car is damaged, the repairer needs a lamp that fits the vehicle exactly, meets road-legal beam requirements, and costs less than the manufacturer's own part.
- **Why it is technically demanding.** A lamp must satisfy **regulatory standards for light output and beam pattern**, be sealed against water and dust, survive years of vibration and thermal cycling, and **match the vehicle's body contours precisely**. Each vehicle model needs its own tooling and optical design. Doing that profitably across hundreds of models is the barrier that keeps the field small, and it is why Depo sustains a **33.5% gross margin** and an **18.3% operating margin** in what sounds like a commodity business.
- **Who benefits from Depo existing.** **Vehicle owners and insurers.** An original manufacturer lamp is expensive; an equivalent independent part reduces the cost of repair and, in aggregate, of insurance. This is why several jurisdictions have adopted **"repair clause"** provisions permitting independent replacement parts.
- **Who does not.** **Vehicle manufacturers**, who earn high margins on original replacement parts and have used **design rights** to defend them — the basis of the **Mercedes-Benz case**, where a second-instance court found infringement and awarded about **NT$18.12m** before the **Supreme Court remanded for retrial**.
- **The financial shape.** Global export sales, so results are exposed to **tariffs and exchange rates** — both cited in FY2025's **26.4% earnings decline**, and the likely context for **2025Q2's 1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin**.

The levers are **vehicle parc size and accident rates, model coverage, tooling investment, currency and trade policy**. The strength is a dominant position in a technically demanding product with structural demand and allies in the insurance industry. The vulnerability is unusual: **Depo's commercial success is directly adverse to the interests of the companies that design the vehicles it serves** — and those companies have legal instruments available to them.

The automotive aftermarket is a large industry defined by a permanent conflict over who supplies replacement parts.

- **The structure.** Vehicles are repaired throughout their lives, and someone must supply the parts. **Original equipment (OEM) parts** come from the vehicle manufacturer at high margin; **aftermarket parts** come from independent producers at substantially lower cost. Insurers, who pay for most collision repairs, have a direct financial interest in the second option.
- **Taiwan's position.** Taiwanese firms — **Depo in lighting, Tong Yang (1319) in sheet metal and bumpers**, both in this collection — built global positions supplying these parts. The competence required is **tooling, fit accuracy and regulatory compliance across hundreds of models**, and Taiwan's manufacturing base proved unusually good at it.
- **The legal battleground.** Carmakers defend their replacement-parts revenue through **design rights**, arguing that a part shaped to fit their vehicle copies their protected design. Independents argue that **the shape is dictated by function** — a lamp must fit the hole — and that many jurisdictions therefore adopt a **repair clause** exempting replacement parts. The European Union has debated this for decades; the **Mercedes-Benz case against Depo** brought it to Taiwan, with a second-instance infringement finding and compensation of about **NT$18.12m**, now **remanded by the Supreme Court for retrial**.
- **Why the sum understates the stakes.** NT$18.12m is trivial against Depo's earnings. **The precedent is not.** A settled ruling that design rights bar independent replacement lamps would reshape the economics of Taiwan's entire aftermarket parts industry — which is why the case has been treated in Taiwan as an industry-level event rather than a company dispute.
- **The demand backdrop.** Aftermarket demand tracks the **size and age of the vehicle fleet** and accident frequency — both stable and slow-moving, which makes the industry considerably less cyclical than new vehicle production.
- **The technology shift.** Lamps have moved from halogen to LED and adaptive systems, raising unit value and technical requirements. That favours capable incumbents and disadvantages low-cost imitators.

Depo's position is **strong operationally and contested legally**. The industry truth is that **the aftermarket exists because original parts are expensive, and the manufacturers who set those prices are also the ones who own the designs** — a conflict that is resolved by legislation and courts, not by competition.

**Strengths**
- **World's largest aftermarket automotive lamp maker**, with tooling and optical capability across hundreds of vehicle models.
- **Strong economics**: gross margin **33.5%**, operating margin **18.3%**, **ROE 10.50%**, operating cash flow **1.8×** net income.
- **Conservative balance sheet**: **36.9% debt ratio**, **NT$3.98bn cash**, **NT$21.1bn equity**.
- **Structural demand** from collision repair, with insurers aligned against high OEM parts pricing.

**Weaknesses**
- **FY2025 EPS fell 26.4%** (NT$18.97 → NT$13.97) on tariffs, currency appreciation and non-operating losses.
- **2025Q2's 1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin** — a large unexplained non-operating charge.
- **Dividend cut** from NT$9.0 to NT$6.5; monthly revenue running **−14% to +8%**.

**Opportunities**
- **Supreme Court remand** and the shift toward competition and repair-rights arguments.
- Legislative **repair-clause** adoption in Taiwan or other markets.
- LED and adaptive lighting raising unit value; growth in the vehicle parc.

**Threats**
- **An adverse final ruling** in the Mercedes design-right case setting an industry-wide precedent.
- **Tariffs and exchange rates** — both already demonstrated in FY2025.
- OEM pressure on insurers and repairers to specify original parts.

- **The litigation precedent, not the damages (the defining risk).** The **NT$18.12m** awarded at second instance is immaterial to Depo's finances. What matters is that a court found that **design rights can bar an independent replacement lamp**. The **Supreme Court has remanded for retrial** and the argument has broadened toward competition and consumer repair rights — a more favourable framing — but the question is unresolved, and an adverse final outcome would affect Depo and the wider Taiwanese aftermarket industry.
- **An unexplained quarter.** **2025Q2 delivered a 1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin**, collapsing EPS to **NT$0.44** while operations remained profitable. A charge of that size is consistent with a large foreign-exchange loss during New Taiwan dollar appreciation, but **the composition was not independently verified and is not asserted here.** Readers should consult company filings.
- **Trade policy and currency.** Depo exports worldwide from a New Taiwan dollar cost base. FY2025's **26.4% earnings decline** was attributed to **tariffs and currency appreciation** alongside non-operating losses — exposures the company can hedge but not remove.
- **Flat demand.** Monthly revenue has run **−14% to +8%** year-on-year. Aftermarket demand is stable rather than growing, so earnings growth must come from mix, pricing or share.
- **The customers' suppliers are the adversaries.** Depo's growth reduces vehicle manufacturers' parts revenue. Those manufacturers control vehicle design, can influence dealer and insurer specification, and hold the intellectual property being litigated.
- **The dividend follows earnings.** **NT$9.0 (FY2024) → NT$6.5 (FY2025)**. The **5.00% yield** reflects the current, lower payout.

Depo's outlook rests on **two things it does not control — a court and a trade policy — and one it does: its margins.** The axes to watch:

- **The Mercedes-Benz case on retrial.** The **Supreme Court remand** reopened a case Depo had lost at second instance, and the argument has shifted toward **whether restricting independent replacement parts is anti-competitive** and what repair rights consumers hold. The eventual ruling matters for the entire Taiwanese aftermarket industry, not just this company.
- **Operating margin, which has held up.** **18.3% in 2026Q1** against 18.6% a year earlier, with gross margin back to **33.5%**. The operations have not deteriorated; the reported earnings did, for reasons below the operating line. Continued stability here is the evidence that FY2025 was a currency and tariff year rather than a business problem.
- **Non-operating items.** After **2025Q2's 1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin**, the gap between operating and net margin is the number to watch each quarter.
- **Revenue direction.** Running **−14% to +8%** monthly. Aftermarket demand is inherently stable, so a sustained return to growth would signal share gains or a richer LED and adaptive-lighting mix.
- **The dividend.** **NT$6.5 for FY2025** from NT$9.0, a roughly 47% payout giving a **5.00% yield**. Recovery in earnings should restore it.

Bottom line: Depo is the **world's largest maker of replacement automotive lamps** — a technically demanding product with structural demand, **33.5% gross margins, 18.3% operating margins, strong cash conversion and a 36.9% debt ratio** — trading at **9.75× earnings and 1.05× book with a 5.00% yield**. It is also a company **sued by Mercedes-Benz over design rights** (infringement found at second instance, about **NT$18.12m**, now **remanded by the Supreme Court**), whose **FY2025 earnings fell 26.4%** on tariffs and currency, and which had **one quarter with a 1.5% net margin against an 18.0% operating margin that public sources do not explain**. Judge it on **operating margin and the litigation's resolution** — an excellent business priced at book because of risks that live outside the factory.
